claim: The Writ's (Éric Grenier) production riding-level projection model blends uniform swing and proportional swing at a fixed 50/50 weight rather than choosing one method.
stance_target: which swing family is used in real-world electoral projection tools
scope_conditions: Canadian federal riding-level projections, model launched March 2026
quoted_support: The riding projection is a 50/50 combination of a proportional and uniform swing model.

claim: Real-world riding-level swing projections are systematically adjusted with discretionary local-factor layers (incumbency, floor-crossing, byelections, absent candidates, leader-in-riding effects) calibrated by backtesting against historical elections, rather than relying on swing alone.
stance_target: swing methods need local adjustment layers to be locally accurate
quoted_support: The size of boosts or penalties assessed is determined by looking at how past actual election results compared to expected results when applying the mixed uniform/proportional swing model to those past elections.

claim: When a party withdraws or fields no candidate in a riding, the model redistributes that candidate's expected share to other parties using fixed empirically-derived proportions rather than zeroing it out -- a direct analogue to French désistement/withdrawal handling.
stance_target: how swing-based models should handle incomplete candidate offers
quoted_support: When a party did not run a candidate in the last election, previous results are used to estimate that party's support.

claim: National/regional vote projections in a production model are built bottom-up as a turnout-weighted sum of riding-level projections, not as a separate top-down polling average -- so local shocks (e.g. an incumbent loss) feed back into the reported national number.
stance_target: how bottom-up local projections should aggregate to a national total
quoted_support: This means that the vote projection takes into account not only turnout dynamics but also the adjustments made to each individual riding. A party losing a large number of incumbents in a province, for example, would be projected to take less of the vote than the polling average would suggest.

claim: Production seat forecasting uses 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations per update, with party- and region-specific polling-error distributions (not symmetric uniform error bands) derived by backtesting 2011-2025 elections.
stance_target: how uncertainty should be quantified in constituency-level seat projections
scope_conditions: Canadian federal riding projections, backtest period 2011-2025
quoted_support: This process is repeated 10,000 times to simulate 10,000 individual election results.

claim: Confidence categories (Safe/Likely/Lean/Close/Edge/Toss) are not based on a uniform vote-margin threshold but vary by party and region because historical polling-error asymmetries differ (e.g. Conservatives have historically beaten their polls more than the NDP).
stance_target: whether a single margin threshold can define seat-safety classifications
quoted_support: Two seats contested by the Conservatives and Liberals with the same margin between the two parties might be an “Edge” call in Ontario and a “Lean” call in Alberta because of how the ranges for the two parties differ from region to region.
